roadmap.goal: Ship slice 06 of ADO Epic #5775 (Story #5781): the published documentation, the compliance self-assessment and the security policy describe what the product actually does, and a prospect's security reviewer can finish their assessment from one URL without asking anyone. Nine slices of code shipped their own documentation as they landed, so six of the twenty criteria are already true and the slice is what no single slice owned: a canonical Security page, the four claims that are still stale, the two facts the security review found were missing, and the pictures of a screen that has been described in prose without one since it shipped.
roadmap.overview: Seven phases, 7 steps. One carries a test - where the in-product link goes. The other six are prose and pictures, each answered by reading the result against a named file. The release-note lines are drafted here and land at the release, because release notes name a version that does not exist yet.

slice_to_phase._not_in_this_roadmap_: the marketing website's security copy, which lives in another repository and is a DELIVER-checklist flag; a GitHub Security Advisory, withdrawn by maintainer decision V7 with AC-6.7; rewriting the Encryption Key section of the configuration reference, which the audit found already true - only two sentences are added to it.

phases.name: One address
phases.description: The gap this epic came from was never a missing claim - it was a missing address. Facts about credential handling exist in a configuration reference, four connector pages, two compliance documents and a repository-root file with no presence in the docs site. None of them is a page anyone would paste into a conversation.

steps.name: The Security page, two layers at one URL
steps.description: Write `docs/security.md` as a new top-level page at `nav_order: 4`, between Licensing and Teams. Above the fold: the plain answer, a few sentences, no algorithm names, the same four facts as the in-product notice - encrypted before saving, never returned to the browser for any role, never leaves the instance, revocable at the source. Below it, a *verify our claims* half: what is encrypted and how, what is deliberately hashed instead and why (API keys, embed session secrets), key custody per deployment shape, what an operator must back up and what is lost if they do not, that upgrading re-encrypts nothing, and a *what this does not protect against* section naming an attacker holding the key, host or shell access, and a malicious administrator. Link the vulnerability reporting path. Then replace the isolated one-liner on each of the four connector concept pages with the plain-language answer and one link here, keeping per-connector specifics where they are. COMMIT: `docs(security): give the question one address`.
steps.test_file: n/a - published prose, asserted by review against AC-6.4, AC-6.12, AC-6.13, AC-6.14, AC-6.15
steps.scenario_name: No scenario - see the DISTILL scenario list for why
criteria: The plain answer is readable by someone who does not know what AES is, and stands alone without the half below it.
The limits section is not softened - a page without it reads as sales copy, which is the failure mode it exists to avoid.
Nothing is duplicated. The scattered mentions become links; per-connector specifics stay on the connector pages.
No claim on the page is false on any supported install, including one still on the published key.

phases.name: The link in the product
phases.description: The notice on the connection form has pointed at an anchor inside the configuration reference since slice 01, because that was the only place the facts existed. It is the one behaviour in this slice a test can reach.

steps.name: Repoint the notice at the page that answers it
steps.description: RED: extend the notice's test - the link resolves to the canonical Security page and not into the configuration reference, and the address does not depend on which work tracking system the form was for. GREEN: change `SECRET_HANDLING_DOCS_URL`. COMMIT: `fix(encryption): send the notice to the page that answers it`.
red_to_green_tests: The notice's link resolves to the Security page
It is not a section inside the configuration reference
The address is the same on every connection form
criteria: The notice's copy is unchanged - only where the link goes.
pnpm test, pnpm build and Biome all clean.

phases.name: The two facts the review found
phases.description: Finding E3: an instance with nowhere to keep a key of its own keeps the published key in force, and every credential entered afterwards goes under it too. The page says such an instance starts and keeps working, which a reader finishes as a statement about the past. The neighbouring gap is the same shape - the upgrade note says the old key is kept for reading and stops there.

steps.name: Say what that instance is running on, and what the upgrade did not do
steps.description: Extend the nowhere-to-keep-a-key section of the configuration reference: the published key stays in force, so new credentials are protected by it as well, and the panel offers that instance no way out because there is nowhere to move anything to - the remedy is one of the two settings. Extend the after-an-upgrade note: an upgrade re-encrypts nothing, so everything stored before it stays under the previously published key, readable by anyone with the source, until a rotation is run. COMMIT: `docs(encryption): say what an instance with nowhere to keep a key is running on`.
steps.test_file: n/a - AC-6.19 and AC-6.17, asserted by review
criteria: The section does not become a warning - it is the same tone as the rest of the page, with one more true sentence.
The two ways out are the two that exist; no third is invented.

phases.name: Where the key lives, per deployment shape
phases.description: Two pages a reader installs from say nothing about the key. The Docker section mounts a data volume and never says the key store belongs on it. The Kubernetes page does not mention encryption at all, while the chart refuses to install without a key - so a reader following that page meets a render failure the page never prepared them for.

steps.name: The Docker volume and the Kubernetes Secret
steps.description: On the server page, state where the key store lives, that it belongs on the mounted data volume, and what recreating the container without that volume costs - the database survives and every stored credential becomes unreadable. On the Kubernetes page, add a custody section: the chart refuses to install without a key, the three ways to own one, the four-step rotation, and that Lighthouse never writes to the Secret itself - by link to the chart README, which already documents the values, rather than restating them where they would drift. COMMIT: `docs(encryption): say where the key lives on Docker and on Kubernetes`.
steps.test_file: n/a - AC-6.11 and AC-6.10, asserted by review
criteria: No chart value is restated on the docs site. The README is the source; the page links it.
The Docker sentence names the cost, not just the rule.

phases.name: The documents a reviewer opens first
phases.description: Before the docs site, a reviewer opens the architecture overview and the compliance file. One describes custody in a subsection of Persistence; the other cites evidence written before any of this shipped, including a row that was false when it was written.

steps.name: Promote the architecture section, re-evidence the compliance rows, date the policy
steps.description: Promote the custody section out of Persistence to sit with the load-bearing concerns, and complete it: the envelope and where it is written, the ring and its resolution at builder time into a singleton, the three custody modes and what each can and cannot be asked to do, where the key store sits relative to the database, and the read-only check and the re-encryption pass as the two things that walk every stored secret. Re-evidence CRA rows 1.3 and 1.5 against the shipped build. Add to the security policy what this epic changed, and move its date. COMMIT: `docs(encryption): put credential protection where a reviewer looks first`.
steps.test_file: n/a - AC-6.18, AC-6.5, AC-6.6, asserted by review
criteria: The architecture section is extended, not re-authored - slice 09 wrote it first and owns its sentences.
Every compliance evidence phrase is checkable against a file in the repository.
Row 1.7's telemetry wording is left alone and stays flagged - it is outside this epic's surface.

phases.name: A picture of the screen
phases.description: The encryption settings page has described that screen in prose since slice 06a and has never shown it. The system information page gained an Encryption row in the same slice, and the committed image predates it. Added at the maintainer's request, 2026-08-17.

steps.name: Screenshot the encryption panel, regenerate system information
steps.description: Add a Page Object for the encryption settings page and a `goToEncryption()` on the settings Page Object, then one `@screenshot` test that captures the panel. Delete the existing system-information image before re-running its test - a regenerated screenshot whose diff is under half a percent is silently kept. Run both locally against a clean backend and check the images before committing; run them by name rather than the whole screenshot suite, so nothing else is regenerated or lost. Reference the new image from the encryption settings documentation page. COMMIT: `docs(encryption): show the screen the page describes`.
criteria: The spec goes through a Page Object - never an inline locator.
The run happens before the commit. An unrun locator is not a deliverable.
No premium-only screenshot test is touched, and the licence-dependent suite is not run.

phases.name: What the release has to say
phases.description: Release notes name a version. The lines are drafted with the slice, while the reasoning is in front of us, and land in the notes for the release that carries slices 01-09.

steps.name: Draft the operator lines the release owes
steps.description: Write the release-note lines into the slice workspace: lead with what the operator should do; state that upgrading re-encrypts nothing already stored; and carry the E3 fact for the shapes that reach it - an install on Postgres, or a container whose database file is not on a mounted volume, that upgrades without setting anything keeps the published key in force for new credentials too. No advisory, per maintainer decision V7. COMMIT: `docs(encryption): draft the release lines this slice owes`.
steps.test_file: n/a - AC-6.8 and AC-6.20, asserted at the release
criteria: The lines lead with the customer's action, not with the mechanism.
They are drafted, not published - the criterion closes when the release ships them.
